transcript:
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
Israel has moved further to tighten restrictions on Palestinians, imposing a week-long closure
of military checkpoints in the occupied West Bank.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reports on the increased Israeli military presence in the territory
ahead of national elections next month.
>> Over the weekend, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said he instructed the military
to impose a "general closure" of the occupied West Bank for the duration of the Jewish holiday.
It's not unusual for Israel to impose further restrictions on Palestinians in the West Bank
during Jewish holidays for what it says are security concerns.
But this comes as Israel has already been significantly building its military presence
in the territory as the election draws closer, and after several recent Palestinian attacks
on Israelis, including one that severely wounded the son of Israel's ambassador to the US.
>> Such closures in the West Bank greatly limit the movement of Palestinians trying
to go about daily life.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
>> The Protect College Sports Act has crossed the finish line in the Senate.
Senators passed a bill late Monday night by a 77 to 22 vote.
Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz was a top negotiator.
>> This bill puts an end to the chaos plaguing college athletics.
It protects NIL opportunities because student athletes deserve the opportunity to benefit
from their talent without being taken advantage of by unscrupulous agents and backdoor deals.
>> The bill establishes a federal framework for college athletics to create one set system
on how athletes can earn money on their name, image, and likeness.
It also caps the amount of money schools can share with their athletes and limits transfers
between schools.
>> President Trump is praising the bill in a social media post following Senate passage.
He said the measure is really a big deal, but it faces uncertainty in the House.
American farmers have largely escaped President Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown.
But as NPR's Kirk Sigler reports, as ice sweeps continue, farmers are growing uneasy because
many still can't find enough workers.
>> Idaho is the nation's third largest milk and dairy producer, and the labor shortage
is even more pronounced in this sector of the farm economy because dairies operate year
round and aren't eligible for coveted H2A seasonal visas.
Rick Nairabout heads the dairy associations for Idaho and Washington State.
>> We haven't seen the worksite enforcement within agriculture, and we've been spared
there for the last year and a half or so.
>> But Nairabout says just as quickly his industry could fall out of favor with the
Trump administration.
Washington had been pushing for a GOP bill that would remove the seasonal requirement
for some farm worker visas, but Congress is now in recess until after the midterms.
Kirk Sigler, NPR News, Twin Falls, Idaho.
>> This is NPR News.
The state of Florida is trying to force open AI to stop developing AI models without third
party safeguards and approval.
NPR's John Ruage reports on the lawsuit the state filed against open AI and its CEO Sam
Altman in June, alleging that the company have put chat GPT on the market while concealing
its risks.
>> In a court filing, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeyer is now seeking a temporary injunction
against open AI.
He posted a video on X explaining what they're asking for.
>> No new model development without independent safety guardrails.
No more harvesting children's data.
No more calling this product safe, accurate or reliable.
>> The filing comes after a wave of incidents at open AI and other AI companies in which
artificial intelligence bots have done things they should not, including escaping test zones
and hacking into other companies and government websites.
Those incidents have raised alarm about AI potentially escaping human control.
Open AI did not respond immediately to an NPR request for comment.
John Ruage, NPR News.
>> Open AI says it's delaying the release of a new artificial intelligence model out
of security concerns.
Open AI's decision Monday comes a day before AI executives are to meet with President Trump
in Washington.
Separately, open AI is apologizing for the hacking of an Australian government website.
That hack was made public last week.
It's the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
Stocks in Asia mixed in Tuesday trading after a down day on Wall Street, the S&P 500 sank
eight tenths of a percent, the Dow dropped seven tenths.
I'm Giles Snyder.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Israel imposes week-long closure of West Bank military checkpoints ahead of elections
Senate passes Protect College Sports Act establishing federal framework for athlete compensation
American farmers growing uneasy about labor shortages despite Trump's immigration crackdown so far
Florida sues OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman over AI safety and data practices
OpenAI delays release of new AI model citing security concerns before Trump meeting
OpenAI apologizes for hacking of Australian government website by AI agent
Asian stocks mixed in Tuesday trading after decline on Wall Street
